title: Glean Enterprise Search and Work AI
positioning: An AI-native enterprise search, assistant, agent, and knowledge platform that connects workplace systems, applies source permissions, builds a company knowledge graph, and helps employees find or act on organizational context.
decisionAngles: Unified enterprise search and assistants versus separate application search, knowledge bases, and workflow tools
Permission-aware retrieval versus connector completeness, source ACL quality, identity mapping, and stale content
Company knowledge graph and enterprise context versus deployment time, taxonomy, governance, and tuning work
Managed agents and workflow automation versus business-process ownership, approvals, auditability, and failure handling
Broad connector ecosystem versus custom-source coverage, sync latency, API limits, and maintenance responsibility
Enterprise security and model flexibility versus legal, regional, hosting, retention, and procurement requirements
Custom enterprise pricing versus measurable adoption, search success, time saved, and total implementation cost

pricingSnapshot.billingUnit: Public pages do not provide a self-serve price card; commercial terms are enterprise-led and can depend on users, products, connectors, deployment scope, services, support, hosting, model choices, and contract commitments.
plans: Enterprise Search and Assistant: organization-wide discovery and AI assistance across connected workplace sources
Agents and automation: configurable workflows and actions built on enterprise context and permissions
Platform and developer capabilities: APIs, connectors, administration, governance, and extensibility
Commercial package: custom quote, implementation, security review, and contract rather than a public self-serve tier
volatileFields: per-user, platform, product, connector, services, support, and contract pricing
connector availability, sync behavior, API access, agent, assistant, and model entitlements
hosting, region, retention, compliance, support, procurement, and implementation terms
usage, seat, indexing, storage, action, and third-party model cost boundaries
pricingSnapshot.releaseGuard: Recheck the live platform, connector, security, legal, and commercial-contact pages on release day; do not invent a public price, free plan, trial, deployment duration, connector SLA, or implementation cost where Glean provides no stable public figure.

policyBoundaries.label: Permission-aware retrieval depends on source and identity integrity
policyBoundaries.summary: Glean is designed to respect source permissions, but correct results still depend on connector configuration, identity mapping, inherited access, source ACLs, and organizational offboarding.
policyBoundaries.releaseGuard: Never describe permission awareness as a substitute for source-system access review; require connector-by-connector ACL, identity, group, guest, and offboarding validation.

policyBoundaries.label: Enterprise context does not make generated answers authoritative
policyBoundaries.summary: Answers and agent actions can combine retrieved context with model reasoning, while sources may be incomplete, stale, conflicting, or misunderstood.
policyBoundaries.releaseGuard: Require citations, source inspection, approval gates, and rollback for consequential answers or actions; do not equate connected context with verified truth.

policyBoundaries.label: Public pricing is intentionally insufficient for cost comparison
policyBoundaries.summary: Glean uses enterprise sales and contractual packaging rather than a stable public self-serve price table.
policyBoundaries.releaseGuard: Mark pricing as custom and compare total deployment scope, not an inferred seat price or unverified third-party quote.

limitations: Value depends on connector coverage, source cleanliness, permissions, identity mapping, indexing freshness, and employee adoption.
Stale, duplicated, contradictory, or poorly governed workplace content can produce confident but unhelpful answers.
Permission-aware retrieval cannot repair incorrect access controls or guest exposure in the underlying source systems.
Enterprise deployment requires security, legal, procurement, integration, taxonomy, change-management, and ownership work.
Public pricing is not available, so total cost and return cannot be assessed without a scoped quote and implementation plan.
Agent actions need approvals, audit logs, least privilege, exception handling, rollback, and accountable process owners.
Custom connectors and less common systems can add engineering work, synchronization delays, API constraints, and maintenance burden.
Search quality and adoption require ongoing query analysis, source curation, feedback loops, training, and governance rather than a one-time rollout.

marketValidation.rationale: Glean has strong enterprise adoption signals, substantial company-reported recurring revenue, broad connector and platform depth, and independent analyst and customer feedback. It has a clear decision role for organizations seeking permission-aware workplace search and AI. Recommendation remains conditional because pricing is opaque, deployment is organizational rather than self-serve, and outcomes depend on source governance, connectors, permissions, adoption, and measurable search quality.
strongSignals: Glean reported surpassing USD 300 million in annual recurring revenue and broad expansion within large enterprises; these figures are company-reported
Gartner Peer Insights maintains verified enterprise customer reviews for Glean in knowledge-management software
The official platform documents enterprise search, assistant, agents, governance, APIs, connectors, security, and model flexibility rather than a narrow experimental chatbot
Independent business reporting has covered Glean's enterprise AI adoption and the implementation work required to make workplace context useful
recurringUserFriction: Organizations report that connector freshness, indexing gaps, source quality, and search tuning strongly affect usefulness
Enterprise pricing and implementation scope are difficult to compare without procurement and a detailed quote
Employees can receive incomplete or misleading answers when source content is stale, duplicated, or poorly governed
Successful rollout requires change management, ownership, permissions cleanup, measurement, and ongoing administration
